comments.author: @JohnK_sempre
comments.text:
Right now, the LLMs the public has access to tends towards just spitting out tokens/words without reflection, error/fact checking, or comparing prospective solutions. It is pretty clear that this is where the failures happen. As Aschenbrenner and others have laid out, if you give System 2 type thinking and tools (e.g., calculators) to LLMs to provide considered thought and planning, and fill in where they are weak we are already very close to AGI with the models we have. 
I find it shocking that people don't grok this. If anything, AI is underhyped on a 10+ year time horizon.

comments.author: @DGPT10
comments.text:
Of course, the hardware, the robots themselves are going to be a bottleneck.. But what if folks were able to help train the AI models by doing the work they already do today, but "remotely". What I mean is, a plumber still plumbs but rather than physically going to the location they remotely control a figure 1 to get in the autonomous plumbing truck, drive the truck to the site Both the figure 1 and the driving model (being trained / running within the truck itself) get trained to drive to the location. Now the figure 1 gets to learn how to navigate to the project, interact with the client and do the actual work of the plumbing using plumbing tools etc. Better yet, the professional operating the figure 1 is not yet a certified plumber but a plumbing student. Not only does the student have a model helping her learn plumbing, giving her advice on which tools to use but she is actively also learning the skill of the remote control and plumbing simultaneously.

A model like this could spread the cost of all of these training, valuable services, and training across all of the participants. The client, the student, figure 1, the vehicle manufacturer, etc. Exciting times.
